sentences.text: Haplocheirus was a small coelurosaur and is classified as a dinosaur.

The genus contains only one species, H. sollers, known from a mostly complete skeleton that includes the skull, and it was identified as an alvarezsaur based on several unambiguous shared traits with that group.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the animal was about 2 meters long and weighed 21 kilograms, while other measurements suggest a length of 1.9 to 2.3 meters and a weight up to 10.56 kilograms.

Haplocheirus differs from derived alvarezsaurids by having heterodont dentition, possessing circular premaxillary teeth without serrations and flattened maxillary teeth with serrations along some of their length.
It retained the ancestral saurischian pubic bone orientation, differing from later alvarezsaurs which evolved an ornithischian-like pubic condition.
The animal possessed a notably robust first finger that was stronger than its second and third fingers.
The single known specimen of Haplocheirus is preserved in near-perfect three-dimensional detail.
Histological examination revealed four lines of arrested growth, indicating the single known specimen of Haplocheirus was approximately four years old at death.
Based on growth curves derived from related species, researchers estimate the adult mass of Haplocheirus to be between 38 kg and 43 kg.

The genus Haplocheirus was described by Choiniere and colleagues in 2010 from a fossil found in rocks dated between 161.2 and 158.7 million years old from the Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of northwestern China.
The type and only specimen of Haplocheirus is designated IVPP V15988 and the only known remains were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.
The slender teeth and lightweight skull of Haplocheirus suggest it primarily fed on small vertebrates.
Large eye orbits and wide scleral apertures suggest that Haplocheirus may have been adapted for nocturnal activity.
Haplocheirus possessed unusually long cochlear canals compared to other non-avian theropods, an adaptation likely linked to enhanced hearing capabilities.
Unlike most alvarezsaurs with highly modified forelimbs, Haplocheirus appears to have used its hands with proficiency comparable to other theropods of similar arm proportions.
Some researchers hypothesize that the robust first finger of Haplocheirus was an adaptation for digging into tree trunks to access insects, similar to the modern aye-aye.

Before Haplocheirus was found, there was a debate over whether alvarezsauroids were closely related to birds or if their similarities were due to convergent evolution, but Haplocheirus suggests that alvarezsauroid ancestry was conventional and not closely related to birds like dromaeosaurs or troodontids.

Some authors argue that Haplocheirus may be more closely related to ornithomimosaurs or that its classification as an alvarezsaur is not robust, while some analyses place Haplocheirus near ornithomimosaurs and researchers note that support for this relationship is stronger than previous hypotheses linking it to avialae.
